standard.title: Electrical energy transformations
standard.description: Explain how electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light in a product or system
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe how forces and the properties of materials affect function in a product or system (AC9TDE4K02). They understand that materials have properties that affect how products work. They have not yet connected electrical energy specifically to output transformations — movement, sound, or light — or worked with circuits as systems.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light in products and systems, and can identify the components needed to control these transformations.

nodes.label: Electrical energy can be transformed into different outputs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that electrical energy can be transformed into movement, sound or light, and give an example of each
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two different outputs that electrical energy can be transformed into (movement, sound, light) and name a product that performs each transformation
nodes.typical_width: Explain how electrical energy is transformed into movement, sound or light across a range of products; describe what component performs the transformation in each case (e.g. motor → movement, speaker → sound, LED → light)
wider: Investigate how automated photovoltaic (solar) systems transform electrical energy to control movement in aquaculture systems — explaining how this creates opportunities for First Nations Australians in coastal northern Australia
Deconstruct a torch or buzzer to identify the components and explain how each contributes to the energy transformation — tracing the path from power source to output
Investigate how sun-tracking solar panels use electrical energy to control movement, and how this improves renewable energy production efficiency in remote communities

response_modes.reason: Students commonly know that electricity 'powers' things but don't think of it as a transformation — energy changing form. Multiple products each showcasing a different transformation output (motor, LED, speaker) help students build the generalisation: electricity in, different form of energy out.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The photovoltaic/aquaculture and solar tracking contexts from the elaborations are genuinely rich — they situate energy transformation in real-world renewable energy systems with social and economic dimensions, rather than just toy examples.
success_criteria: Names at least two different outputs of electrical energy transformation
Identifies the component that performs the transformation in at least one product
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify that electrical energy transforms into different outputs cannot reason about which components to select or arrange in N2 — the planning and control task in N2 requires knowing what transformation is needed.

nodes.label: Planning and controlling a system to produce a specific output
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how components in a circuit or system are selected and arranged to produce and control a specific output (movement, sound or light)
nodes.minimum_width: Plan the components needed for a simple circuit that produces one specific output; explain the role of each component (power source, switch, output device)
nodes.typical_width: Plan and select components for a system to perform a specific task; explain how switches, power sources and output components work together; describe how the arrangement of components controls the output (e.g. controlling movement with a switch, varying light with different resistors)
wider: Construct or model a system that controls movement, sound or light — e.g. an automaton, a pulley-based lifting system, or a circuit in a security system — explaining how each component contributes to the overall output

Investigate the properties of materials that affect a circuit's output — for example, how the reflectivity of a surface affects a light sensor in a security system — connecting material properties to system performance

response_modes.reason: Component selection is a reasoning task — students must work backwards from the desired output to the components needed. The reasoning chain (what output is needed? → what component produces it? → what controls it? → what powers it?) prevents students from listing components without understanding their roles.

This node integrates individual component knowledge into a working system understanding. The switch, power source and output device must be understood as a coordinated system, not separate items — the integration act is designing for a specific, controlled output.

success_criteria: Identifies the components needed for a circuit producing a specific output
Explains the role of each component in the system
